title: MoE: why huge models run on small graphics cards
deck: Having many parameters does not mean using many parameters at every step.
prereq: Chapter 1. Knowing what a token and VRAM are is enough; Chapters 3 and 4 help with the "Go deeper" section.
goals: Explain what an expert is and how the router picks experts
Estimate how many parameters one token really uses
Explain how Strata splits the experts between the GPU and RAM

quiz.text: Each layer has 512 experts and picks only 10 each time. Can we just delete the experts that were not picked?
choices: Yes, they were not used this time anyway
No, the next token may need them
Only if the router is accurate enough
quiz.why: Sparse computation is not permanent pruning. Deleting experts changes the model itself; the upstream Coder version dropped half of the experts and got clearly weaker at Chinese.

quiz.text: If more experts are cached on the GPU, what usually happens to generation speed?
choices: It goes up: the CPU has fewer missed experts to compute
No change: speed depends only on GPU compute
It goes down: VRAM is fuller
quiz.why: In upstream measurements, raising the experts on the GPU from 1,589 to 3,872 lifted the speed from 50.9 to 62.6 tokens per second.

quiz.text: The 10th and 11th experts differ in score by only 0.0001. What can a tiny numerical error in the computation do?
choices: Nothing, the error is too small
It can swap out a whole expert
The output will also differ by only 0.0001
quiz.why: Top-k is a discontinuous boundary: however small the score gap, once the ranking flips, a different expert takes part in the computation.

problem: You have a 12 GB graphics card and plan to switch to a 24 GB one. Using "each extra 1 GB of VRAM holds about 700 more experts", how many more experts can you cache? Will speed necessarily rise in proportion? List at least two factors that could make the estimate wrong.
answer: The extra 12 GB holds about 12 × 700 = 8,400 more experts. But speed will not rise in proportion: (1) VRAM must also hold the chat history (KV), the weights used at every step such as attention, and scratch buffers, and a long context eats more VRAM; (2) the gain depends on the hit rate: when the hot experts are already on the GPU, the new ones are mostly cold, so returns diminish; (3) the bottleneck may move to the CPU, RAM bandwidth or the GPU's own compute; (4) experts differ in size across quantization formats, so the count per GB differs too. The only way to know the real gain is to measure with a fixed model, context length and workload.

title: PLE and n-grams: the model looks things up in a big table too
deck: Hashing to row numbers, reading the SSD by page, an 8-way set-associative row cache: how a 28.8 GB table gives up only 16 rows per token.
prereq: Chapter 1 (memory hierarchy) and Chapter 10 (intuition for experts and caching). A little binary helps.
goals: Explain what an n-gram is, and how three tokens become 16 row numbers through hashing (multiply, XOR, take the remainder)
Work out the cost of reading by page: why a 90-byte row needs a 4 KiB read, and why a row that crosses a page boundary needs two pages
Use set-associative caches and a rotating pointer to explain conflict misses: why a cache with enough total capacity can still keep missing

quiz.text: When a set in Strata's PLE row cache is full, which row gets replaced?
choices: The row that has gone unused the longest
The row under this set's replacement pointer; then the pointer moves on by one
A row picked at random
quiz.why: The source gives each set a rotating pointer: the new row is written into the way the pointer points at, the pointer adds one, and after a full round it wraps to the start. It does not track which row was used most recently, so it is not LRU.

quiz.text: A row is 200 bytes and starts at byte 4000 of a page (4096 bytes). Reading whole pages, how many pages must be read?
choices: 1 page
2 pages
200 pages
quiz.why: 4000 + 200 = 4200, past the page's end at 4096. The row reaches into the next page, so both pages must be read.

quiz.text: Two different trigrams hash to the same row. What happens?
choices: The program reports an error and refuses to run
Both read the same row data; this is a collision accepted by design
The program automatically stores one of them in an empty row instead
quiz.why: The table stores only values, not keys, so it neither notices nor handles collisions. There are far more combinations than rows, so collisions are certain. Different heads use different moduli, so two n-grams rarely collide on every head.

problem: A program hands its SSD reads to a dedicated I/O thread. The time the main thread spends submitting requests drops to almost zero, yet the total time per token does not get shorter. Give two reasonable explanations, and say what to measure to tell them apart.
answer: Explanation 1: right after submitting, the main thread needs the data, with no other work to do in between. The waiting has only moved from "submit" to "collect"; it has not been hidden. Explanation 2: the reads themselves got slower or are held up by something else, such as the cost of waking threads and taking locks, the latency of random reads, or the same file still being memory-mapped, which serializes the reads. To tell them apart, record three timestamps for every request: submitted, completed and consumed. If completion comes well before consumption, the reads are already hidden and the bottleneck is elsewhere. If the consumer is always waiting for completion, look at the percentiles of the wait time and of the single-read latency.

title: The expert cache: whom to keep, how to split, when to swap
deck: The denominator of a hit rate, a starting list ranked by frequency, a range of slots per layer, replacement by decayed count, and the "copy first, register after" order of a swap.
prereq: Chapter 10 (the intuition behind MoE and the expert cache) and Chapter 11 (set-associative caches).
goals: Name the denominator of a hit rate, and explain why the per-expert hit rate and the whole-layer hit rate differ by more than ten times
Compare LRU, LFU and decayed counts, and state the adjustment rules of Strata's expert cache (every 4 rounds, a count of 2, a lead of 1.5, × 0.7)
Write down the correct order for one swap: remove the table entry, wait for the copy to finish, then register

quiz.text: In some layer, each expert's hit rate is 70%. If the experts were independent, about how likely is it that all 10 experts in this layer hit?
choices: About 2.8%
quiz.why: All 10 must hit: 0.7 to the 10th power ≈ 0.028. The two metrics have different denominators and cannot stand in for each other. Real routing is not independent, so the real figure has to be measured separately.

quiz.text: During an expert swap, the residency table already says "#112 is in slot 5", but the bytes are still being copied. If the GPU follows the table and computes #112 now, what happens?
choices: Nothing wrong, just a bit slower
It may read half-new, half-old bytes and compute a wrong result without any error
The program is sure to crash
quiz.why: The table entry and the bytes must be valid together. When an async copy function returns, the bytes have not necessarily arrived; registering early creates a fake hit with "right label, wrong bytes". The output looks normal, but it is already wrong.

quiz.text: The early expert cache had all layers share one counter and handed out slots in order of arrival. Its hit rate was only about 3%. What was the main reason?
choices: VRAM was too small
The early layers arrived first and took every slot, so the later layers never got any
The GPU cannot compute the later layers
quiz.why: A token walks from layer 0 onward, and 256 slots are all handed out by about layer 26. Capacity was enough; the problem was that allocation got tangled up with the access order. Giving each layer its own range of slots fixed it.

problem: In the low-RAM resident mode, RAM holds only the experts the graphics card does not have. List three conditions that one expert swap in this mode must keep.
answer: First, before the incoming expert becomes visible to the GPU (registered in the residency table), its bytes have been fully copied into the VRAM slot. Second, before its slot is overwritten, the outgoing expert has been removed from the table (the CPU computes it from then on), and its full bytes have been copied back to RAM, into the place the incoming expert used to hold, so the RAM copy keeps exactly filling in what the GPU is missing. Third, table changes are synchronized with concurrent readers: any token that picks either expert during the copy must take the CPU path and must never see a half-new, half-old state. You should also check that expert blocks never cross slot boundaries, that errors can roll back, and that the RAM budget is not exceeded.

title: CPU + GPU: parallel within a layer, in line across layers
deck: Computing an expert is mostly reading bytes. Hits go to the GPU and misses to the CPU, both at once; data dependence sets the critical path.
prereq: Chapter 5 (intuition for bandwidth and the critical path), Chapter 10 (MoE) and Chapter 12 (the expert cache).
goals: Describe how CPUs and GPUs are designed differently, and use the SIMD example to explain why only independent data can be computed at once
Explain why Strata lets the CPU compute missed experts in place, and draw the timeline of how the GPU and CPU share one layer
Use data dependence and the critical path to explain why layers cannot run in parallel, and why cutting work that is not on the critical path does nothing

quiz.text: The two branches are independent. The CPU branch has an effective rate Bc = 40 and the PCIe branch Bp = 20. To make both finish at the same time, what fraction f should go to the PCIe branch?
quiz.why: Set the two times equal: (1 − f)/40 = f/20, which gives f = 20 ÷ (40 + 20) = 1/3. The slower branch should get the smaller share.

quiz.text: While the CPU is still computing layer l's experts, can the GPU start computing layer l + 1?
choices: Always
No, layer l + 1's input must wait for layer l to finish merging
Yes, as long as there are enough threads
quiz.why: Layer l + 1's input is exactly layer l's result after its 10 experts are merged. That is a data dependence. No scheduler, however clever, can get around it; the 48 layers form one serial chain.

quiz.text: Upstream cut the CPU's expert work per token from 18.2 milliseconds to 10.2 milliseconds, yet the total time per token did not change. What is the most likely reason?
choices: The CPU measurement was wrong
The GPU's share of the work was queued behind the CPU, so the critical path stayed just as long
Not enough VRAM
quiz.why: In the first version, the GPU step that computes the hit experts ran after the CPU expert pool, so the GPU's share filled the time the CPU saved. Only after both sides computed at once did it really get faster.

problem: Build an example where giving a larger share to the GPU makes the whole thing slower. Explain it with the times of the two branches.
answer: Say that in some layer the CPU branch takes 8 milliseconds and the GPU branch over PCIe takes 7 milliseconds, so the join is set by the CPU's 8 milliseconds. Move more missed experts to the GPU: the CPU drops to 4 milliseconds, but the GPU branch grows to 12 milliseconds (PCIe transfer is slow), so the join now comes at 12 milliseconds, slower than before. If you also account for the CPU reading experts and PCIe reading pinned memory sharing the same memory bandwidth, a longer GPU branch also slows the CPU down, and things get even worse. The best point is where the two branches finish at the same time, not "the more GPU, the better".

title: Pinned memory, DMA and async: copy while you compute
deck: Virtual addresses can move, but DMA trusts only physical addresses; "submitted" does not mean "done"; double buffering is correct only thanks to two signals.
prereq: Chapter 6 (files and memory mapping), Chapter 12 (swapping experts in the cache), Chapter 13 (how the CPU and GPU split the work).
goals: Use virtual memory and paging to explain why DMA needs pinned memory and why Strata pins tens of GB at startup
Tell synchronous from asynchronous calls, and name two "returned does not mean done" examples in Strata (cache fills, verify window commits)
Compute the total time of double buffering and state what makes it correct: read only after the copy is done, write only after it has been used

quiz.text: An asynchronous copy function has returned. What does that tell you?
choices: The data has definitely reached its destination
The copy has been submitted, not necessarily finished
The source buffer can be freed right away
quiz.why: An asynchronous call only hands the work off. Whether the data has arrived, and whether the source buffer can be changed, depends on the completion event, not on whether the function has returned.

quiz.text: Two buffers, 4 chunks, each chunk takes 3 milliseconds to copy and 5 to compute, and copy and compute use independent hardware. What is the ideal total time?
choices: 20 milliseconds
23 milliseconds
32 milliseconds
quiz.why: The first copy takes 3 milliseconds, the 3 steps in between each cost the slower compute, 5 milliseconds, and the last compute takes 5: 3 + 3 × 5 + 5 = 23. Only a fully serial run takes 4 × 8 = 32.

quiz.text: The GPU can read a block of pinned memory directly through a mapping. Does that mean the data is already in VRAM?
choices: Yes
No, every read still goes over PCIe
Only on Windows
quiz.why: "An address the GPU can access" and "where the data actually lives" are two different things. Mapped pinned memory still sits in the host's RAM; the GPU reads it over PCIe and is limited by the bus bandwidth.

problem: A program sometimes reads the previous round's old state when it saves a checkpoint. Someone added "wait 0.1 seconds" before the save, and the problem went away. Why is this not a reliable fix? What should be done instead?
answer: A fixed wait does not create an explicit "read only after the write is done" relationship. On a slower machine, under resource contention, or when this round has more data, 0.1 seconds may not be enough and the problem comes back; on a fast machine it just wastes time. The right fix is to wait for the completion signal tied to that state write, such as an event recorded after the write, or the wait_commit() that Strata's verifier provides, and to handle a failed or timed-out wait.

title: GPU kernels, fusion and CUDA Graph
deck: Every kernel launch pays a check-in fee: how do you check in less without freezing the position?
prereq: Chapters 1, 5 and 13 (the memory hierarchy, bandwidth, and how the CPU and GPU differ).
goals: Explain how threads, thread blocks and warps divide the work, and why neighboring threads should read neighboring addresses
Use n × L + w and L + n × w to judge whether a chain of kernels is limited by launch overhead
Tell kernel fusion apart from CUDA Graph, and explain why values that change every step must live in a fixed-address buffer when you capture a graph

quiz.text: A kernel computes for only 5 microseconds, but each submission takes 20 microseconds. If you submit 45 such kernels one by one, what is the GPU doing most of the time?
choices: Computing at full load the whole time
Waiting for the CPU to submit the next kernel
Waiting for data in VRAM to move to the SSD
quiz.why: When w < L, the total is about n × L + w = 45 × 20 + 5 = 905 microseconds, of which the GPU computes only 45 × 5 = 225 microseconds; the rest is spent waiting for submissions. This is what "launch-bound" means.

quiz.text: Are CUDA Graph and kernel fusion the same thing?
choices: Yes, a graph merges all kernels into one
No: a graph saves CPU-side submission and its nodes are still the original kernels; fusion is what merges the computation into one kernel
They are the same compiler optimization under different names
quiz.why: A graph records a chain of operations and their dependencies, then submits and replays the whole chain at once, and each node still runs on its own. Fusion rewrites the kernel so intermediate results stay on chip. Strata uses both.

quiz.text: If you capture "the current position pos" into a graph as a kernel argument and then simply replay it, what happens?
choices: The driver adds one to pos automatically
Every token writes to position 0, the value at capture time; the program reports no error, but the model acts as if it has lost its memory
The graph refuses to replay and reports an error
quiz.why: A graph copies argument values at capture time, and replay never rereads them. Strata's qsa.hpp puts pos, n_kv, n_bid and width into a fixed-address step buffer; the kernels read it from VRAM every time, and the host rewrites its content each step.

problem: Design a small test that does not need the full large model and that catches the bug "sampling parameters are not updated when the graph is replayed".
answer: Fix a set of logits and send two requests in a row: the first greedy, the second at high temperature or with a different fixed random number. Run each on both the graph path and a reference path that does not use a graph, and compare the parameters each path actually used and the tokens it picked. The second request must take a branch that differs from the first and can be predicted. If you only change the random seed while the distribution is so lopsided that it always picks the same token, this test cannot reveal the bug.

title: Prefill: turning many tokens into a batch problem
deck: On the same computer, reading the prompt is more than twenty times faster than writing the answer: the secret is batching and pipelining.
prereq: Chapters 3, 5, 10 and 14 (matrix multiplication, bandwidth and arithmetic intensity, MoE experts, DMA and asynchrony).
goals: Use matrix × vector vs matrix × matrix to explain why prefill is faster than decode
Explain grouping by expert and the trade-offs of chunk size C: reuse, temporary VRAM, cancel latency
Draw the pipeline that overlaps moving and computing, and name the states that must be handed off after a chunk

quiz.text: During prefill every token of the prompt is already known. So can the 5th token "see" the 6th?
choices: Yes, they are all known anyway
No. The causal rule does not change; batching only changes how the computation is organized
Only for English prompts
quiz.why: A known input does not mean the model may look at the future. Prefill still uses the causal mask, and the recurrent layers still walk through the chunk in order.

quiz.text: Why does the dense part for 8 tokens together take only about 3 times as long as for one token, and not 8 times?
choices: Because the GPU skips half of the tokens
Because one read of the weights is shared by all 8 tokens, so the moving cost is spread thin
Because computing together uses lower precision
quiz.why: In matrix × vector, one read of the weights serves one token; in matrix × matrix, the same weights serve the whole batch. The compute is all still done, but the move is paid once. The default table in spec/controller.hpp lists 3.0× for 8 tokens.

quiz.text: During prefill, Strata puts the chunk buffer in slots borrowed from the expert cache. While prefill runs, can the experts that used to be in those slots still count as "hits"?
choices: Yes, the address has not changed
No. Their bytes have been overwritten, so they must be moved instead and filled back in after prefill
Yes, as long as the budgets add up to less than VRAM
quiz.why: The address is still there, but the content is now the chunk buffer. The safety condition is that at every moment the label matches the bytes in the slot: while lent out they do not count as hits, and only after the refill finishes may they be announced again.

problem: The same prompt is read once with C = 1 and once with C = 8192, and the final answers are not word-for-word identical. Why can you neither conclude right away that one side has a bug, nor wave it off with "it's just floating point"?
answer: Batched and one-by-one computation can take different rounding paths (upstream has documented that IQ models round differently in the single-token and multi-token expert kernels), and a tiny logits difference can make some token branch off. But the difference can also come from a real error in the state handoff, the causal mask or the layout. Compare on the same fixed history: the intermediate tensors, the chosen experts and index numbers, and the layer where the error starts to grow. Then judge by tolerances and quality gates set in advance. Check the non-numeric contracts, such as state positions, the mask and index numbers, separately and exactly.

title: KV capacity, working sets and tiered storage
deck: How many bytes does it take to remember a conversation, is that GB or GiB, and does it live in VRAM or RAM?
prereq: Chapters 1, 4, 8 and 12 (memory hierarchy, quantization, attention, cache replacement).
goals: Compute the KV bytes of one conversation as 12 layers × 2 heads × 256 dimensions × 2 × bytes per element
Tell GB (10⁹) from GiB (2³⁰), and spot errors where the number and the unit do not match
Explain the page table and KV streaming: VRAM holds only the pages in use, the full history is in RAM, and misses are swapped in with CLOCK

quiz.text: When Strata stores KV in FP16, how big is the main KV for a 128K (131,072-token) context?
choices: Exactly 3 GiB
12 GiB
108 MiB
quiz.why: 12 layers × 2 heads × 256 dimensions × 2 (K, V) × 2 bytes = 24,576 bytes per token; times 131,072 that is 3,221,225,472 bytes, exactly 3 × 2³⁰, which is 3 GiB (about 3.22 GB).

quiz.text: How should you write 805,306,368 bytes?
choices: 805 MiB
805 MB, which is 768 MiB
768 MB
quiz.why: Divide by 10⁶ to get 805.3 MB, or by 2²⁰ to get 768 MiB. A comment in Strata's source writes "805 MiB", pairing the decimal number with the binary unit.

quiz.text: A 256K conversation runs with KV streaming on, and VRAM keeps the KV of only 32,768 positions. Can the model still see the earlier content?
choices: No, the earlier history has been deleted
Yes: the full history is in RAM, and selected pages are swapped into VRAM before they are read
It can see only 1 in every 4 tokens
quiz.why: Being resident and being kept are two different things. The upstream docs say that with streaming, attention reads exactly the same values; only where the KV lives changes. How much stays in VRAM affects only speed.

problem: A report counts Strata's KV over 48 layers and says "this is a conservative estimate, so it is fine". Why does the report still fail?
answer: Only the 12 QSA layers have KV, so counting 48 layers makes the result 4 times too big. Erring on the safe side is not the same as having the right model: a false attribution makes people misjudge the bottleneck, buy the wrong hardware or switch off useful features. Count with the real 12 layers, then list the margin as its own item, instead of passing off a structural error as margin.

title: Speculative decoding: guess boldly, commit strictly
deck: Guess a few tokens, then verify them in one go: how is a wrong guess taken back, and why does the answer stay the same?
prereq: Chapters 2, 9, 14 and 16 (sampling and random numbers, the GDN recurrent state, synchronous versus asynchronous, batching).
goals: State the rule "accept up to the first mismatch" and explain why every draft after it is thrown away
Map speculative decoding onto CPU branch prediction and speculative execution
Say, state by state, how GDN, the indexer, PLE and KV are taken back when the first a + 1 rows are committed

quiz.text: In the window, the 2nd draft differs from the target's pick, and the 3rd draft happens to match the original text. Can the 3rd one be accepted?
choices: Yes, it is right
No, it was guessed after a wrong word, so its premise no longer holds
It depends on how long the window is
quiz.why: Correctness holds as a chain along the prefix: a later draft has a correct premise only if everything before it matched. Strata's loop while (window[a+1] == outv[a]) ++a stops at the first mismatch.

quiz.text: With temperature sampling on, how does Strata decide whether a draft can be accepted?
choices: The draft writes for the target directly, with no verification
Only if it exactly equals the target's reproducible sampled result for this row
Accept it with probability min(1, p/q)
quiz.why: Each row's random number is set by the seed and the absolute position, and the draft must equal the target's sampled result for that row. min(1, p/q) is the classic paper's method, not the Strata code this book read.

quiz.text: A window accepted only 1 draft. Is it enough to just roll back the position counter?
choices: Yes
No: GDN must replay, the indexer must restore a snapshot, and PLE must restore the matching snapshot
Only KV needs handling
quiz.why: Different states are taken back in different ways. The extra KV slots actually need nothing and wait to be overwritten next round; GDN, the indexer and PLE each return to the prefix state in their own way.

problem: You want to add a "per-sequence statistics buffer" to Strata (for example, one that counts how often each token has appeared). Write a speculative-decoding safety checklist for it.
answer: ① Which range of the history it covers; ② whether the verify window writes it tentatively while running; ③ whether it needs a snapshot, replay of recorded inputs, or is naturally overwritable; ④ how commit(n_keep) makes it reflect only the first n_keep rows (note n_keep = accepted drafts + 1); ⑤ how the rejected part is invalidated; ⑥ who confirms that asynchronous reads and writes have finished, and with which event (for example wait_commit after an asynchronous commit); ⑦ how it is cleaned up on an end token, a cancellation or a session restore; ⑧ compare it item by item with the reference result without speculation under the same fixed history.

title: How many drafts to guess: expected value, cost and learning on the fly
deck: A correctly guessed token is free, but verification takes time. How many guesses pay off best, and what if the acceptance rate changes?
prereq: Chapter 18 (speculative decoding and commit). Chapter 10's expert cache helps but is not required.
goals: Use conditional acceptance rates to compute the expected tokens committed per round, and explain why extra guesses give diminishing returns
Explain why you compare "expected tokens committed per millisecond" rather than the acceptance rate or the window length
Estimate a changing acceptance rate with an exponential moving average, and handle draft positions that were never compared correctly

quiz.text: Three drafts have conditional acceptance rates 0.8, 0.6 and 0.5. How many tokens does one round commit on average?
quiz.why: E = 1 + 0.8 + 0.8×0.6 + 0.8×0.6×0.5 = 1 + 0.8 + 0.48 + 0.24 = 2.52. The leading 1 is the big model's own token; draft i is useful only if the first i are all accepted.

quiz.text: A round guessed 3 and the 1st was rejected right away. How should the estimate for position 3 be updated?
choices: Record a failure
Do not update: it was never compared this round
Record a success
quiz.why: Once the 1st draft is rejected, later positions are not compared; the outcome is "not seen". Recording a failure drags the deep positions' estimates down, and the controller wrongly concludes long windows do not pay. Strata's observe updates only the accepted positions and the first rejected one.

quiz.text: When the controller picks a window length, which number does it really want to maximize?
choices: The number of drafts
The drafts' acceptance rate
Expected tokens committed ÷ time per round
quiz.why: The goal is more tokens per millisecond. As the window grows, the expected token count grows more and more slowly while the round time keeps rising, so speed has a peak. A high acceptance rate with more expensive rounds can still be slower overall.

problem: Strata's controller updates acceptance rates with an exponential moving average using α = 0.05. What would happen with α = 0.5 instead? Explain in terms of reaction speed and noise, and compute the half-life for both values of α.
answer: Half-life = ln 0.5 ÷ ln(1 − α). That is about 13.5 rounds for α = 0.05 and exactly 1 round for α = 0.5. With α = 0.5 the estimate catches up almost immediately after a topic change, but every acceptance or rejection makes it jump a lot (the steady-state standard deviation is about √(α ÷ (2 − α) × p(1 − p)), which at p = 0.86 rises from about 0.056 to about 0.20). The controller would change windows constantly, and a few chance rejections could even push the estimate below the threshold and stop drafting. Looking only at Controller's two functions, once drafting stops there are no new observations, so the estimate can never recover. α is a trade-off between "react fast" and "do not get fooled by noise".

title: Prefix reuse, snapshots and copy-on-write
deck: Why does a follow-up answer almost instantly? The engine saved the prefix it already read. But "the same question" is not "the same state", and saving the KV is not saving the whole conversation.
prereq: Chapters 9, 17 and 18. Knowing what the KV cache and recurrent state are is enough.
goals: Name the four conditions prefix reuse must meet: steering mode, length, tokens and image identity
Explain why the KV cache can roll back by "ignoring the later rows" while the recurrent state can only roll back through checkpoints
Use copy-on-write to count how many pages two branches sharing a prefix must copy, and state what Strata actually does

quiz.text: Two requests have exactly the same token IDs; only the image attached to the second one is different. Will Strata reuse the first one's checkpoint?
choices: Yes, the tokens are the same
No, the image's position and hash must also match
Yes, as long as both images have the same size
quiz.why: In the token sequence an image is just a run of placeholders, and identical placeholders can stand for completely different pictures. The engine records each image's start position and content hash separately; a different hash means no reuse.

quiz.text: You want to take a conversation back to its state at token 4. Which kind of memory can roll back by simply "ignoring what comes after", and which cannot?
choices: The KV cache can, the GDN recurrent state cannot
Both can
The GDN recurrent state can, the KV cache cannot
quiz.why: The KV cache appends one row per position, and the later rows will be overwritten later, so ignoring them works. The GDN recurrent state is rewritten whole and in place for every token, so its old form is gone; only a checkpoint saved in advance can bring it back.

quiz.text: The prefix has 17 tokens at 4 per page, and after the fork both A and B keep writing. With copy-on-write, how many KV pages must at least be copied after the fork?
choices: 0 pages
1 page
5 pages
quiz.why: The first 4 pages are full and only read, never written, so they can be shared. Page 5 holds only 1 prefix token and both sides will write into it, so whoever writes first must copy it. Only a full copy would need 5 pages.

problem: Design a minimal experiment that needs no GPU to check whether "session A saves a snapshot, switches to run B, then restores A" leaks state between the sessions.
answer: Use a deterministic toy recurrence (for example s ← 0.5s + t). Give A and B the same prefix, then different suffixes, and advance them in turns: run A a few steps and save a snapshot, switch to B, then restore A and continue. At every step compare A's and B's states bit for bit with the result of "replaying each one independently from the start"; they must be exactly equal. Then add some failures: A is cancelled midway and B continues, a snapshot is truncated, a snapshot has the wrong format, the budget is too small. The correct response is to refuse clearly and keep the original state, not to carry on computing with half a state.

title: Two graphics cards: layer split, pipelining and handoff
deck: Two graphics cards first solve "it does not fit", not "it is too slow": a token still queues layer by layer, and the pipeline only starts turning while reading the prompt.
prereq: Chapters 1, 5, 10 and 16; having read Chapter 18's "verify window" helps.
goals: Tell apart what a layer split, tensor parallelism and request parallelism each save and each cost
Use a + b + (N − 1) × max(a, b) to compute a pipeline's total time and its bubbles
Estimate the cost of a handoff from the bytes, the number of crossings and the bandwidth

quiz.text: The first card needs 4 ms for its layers and the second 5 ms, ignoring transfers. Generating just one token, what is the fastest it can take?
choices: 5 ms
9 ms
4.5 ms
quiz.why: The same token must finish the first card's layers before it can enter the second card, so the two parts can only run one after the other: 4 + 5 = 9 ms. The two cards cannot work on the same token at once.

quiz.text: Still 4 ms and 5 ms, the prompt is cut into 8 chunks, and the two cards read staggered. About how long does it take?
choices: 44 ms
72 ms
40 ms
quiz.why: The slower card sets the beat: total = 4 + 5 + (8 − 1) × 5 = 44 ms. 72 ms is chunk after chunk in sequence; 40 ms ignores the fill bubble at the start.

quiz.text: Why does Strata's two-card mode not need NVLink?
choices: It crosses cards only once per verify window, with only a few hundred KB of data
It splits every layer's matrices across both cards and computes them at the same time
Each card serves different users and they never talk
quiz.why: Strata uses a layer split: a token crosses cards once per verify window, 51,216 bytes per token, relayed through RAM, and PCIe is enough. Syncing at every layer is what tensor parallelism does, and that is what needs a fast interconnect.

problem: A friend says: "I added a second graphics card and prompt reading got 20% faster, which shows the layer-split pipeline is very efficient." What is loose about this reasoning? How would you measure it?
answer: The extra VRAM can cache more experts and cut CPU work, which by itself speeds things up and has nothing to do with the pipeline. Measure separately: each card's expert hit rate, the CPU pool's workload, the handoff time, and each stage's time per chunk. Then use a + b + (N − 1) × max(a, b) to estimate the pure pipeline's theoretical gain and compare it with the measurement. You can also compare with "no split when one card is enough" (upstream's split_skip_if_fits switch) to see how much comes from capacity and how much from the pipeline.

title: Portability: one source tree, different machines
deck: A chip understands only its own instructions. One source tree must be compiled once for each kind of machine, and "it compiles" is still several levels of evidence away from "it is supported".
prereq: Chapters 10 and 13. Knowing that the GPU and the CPU split the expert computation is enough; Chapter 4's floating-point rounding helps with Section 22.4.
goals: Explain what the compiler, the instruction set and conditional compilation each do, and read a block of #if branches
Explain how Strata picks AVX-512 / AVX2 kernels at run time on the CPU, and how it builds CUDA-style source into a HIP engine
Tell apart four levels of evidence (compiles, tests pass, runs on a real card, maintainer verified) and write a support statement that does not overclaim

quiz.text: Strata adds the AVX-512 compile switch only to a few kernel source files, not to the whole program. What is the main reason?
choices: To make compiling faster
So the CPU probe and the fallback code can run safely on CPUs without AVX-512
Because AVX-512 instructions may appear in only one file
quiz.why: Once a file is compiled with the AVX-512 switch, the compiler may insert AVX-512 instructions anywhere in it. Keeping the probe and the fallback in files without the switch lets an old CPU safely "ask first" and then decide which path to take.

quiz.text: How does Strata's HIP build get CUDA-style source to compile for AMD cards?
choices: A tool permanently rewrites every source file into HIP
At compile time it force-includes a shim header whose macros rename cuda-prefixed names to hip names, and it hand-writes a few built-in functions HIP lacks
AMD cards can run NVIDIA machine code directly
quiz.why: The build script uses -include to push hip_compat/cuda_runtime.h into every source file; it holds 82 lines of #define renaming, and built-ins such as __dp4a and warp shuffles are implemented separately per GPU architecture in intrinsics.hpp. The source itself is not changed.

quiz.text: gfx1102 compiles and passes Strata's built-in tests. By this chapter's evidence levels, which statement is most accurate?
choices: It is fully supported
It has two levels of evidence, compiling and tests, but no report of a complete model run yet, so it still counts as unverified
It cannot be used because it is on no list
quiz.why: The build script lists gfx1102 as unverified: it compiles, and configuring prints a warning. Passing tests shows the kernels do not crash and compute correctly, but a real model running on a real card, reproduced by someone, is a higher level of evidence.

problem: You added a new GPU backend to Strata and ran one decode successfully on one card with one model pack. Write a support statement that does not overclaim, listing at least the build conditions to record, the scope that was verified, and the parts explicitly not tested.
answer: Build conditions: the source commit, the compiler and its version, the list of target architectures, every compile switch, the dependency library versions (such as the pinned ggml commit), and the runtime environment variables. Verified scope: the device model and driver, the model pack and quantization format, the KV format, whether only decode or also prefill was tested, the context length and how many tokens were run; label the evidence level clearly as "compiles", "built-in tests pass", "tensor-level error against a reference implementation" or "end-to-end quality". Untested parts: list other architectures, other model packs, long contexts, multiple GPUs, another operating system and so on, one by one, as "untested". Do not write "fully supported", and do not promise bit-identical results with other backends.
